info.bio:
Paul Whiteman, también llamado Pops, (Denver, 28 de marzo de 1880 - Doylestown, 29 de diciembre de 1967) director de orquesta estadounidense y músico de Jazz, alcanzó junto a su formación la Whaiteman Band gran popularidad en los años 1920 por sus trabajos en el mundo de las variedades y el Music Hall. En 1924 dirigió el estreno de la obra Rhapsody in Blue que había encargado al compositor Georges Gershwin.

Por su grupo se dieron a conocer solistas como Bing Crosby

scenes.name: Orquestas de baile: Whiteman y Goldkette
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: Músicas «en los intersticios» que las historias del jazz desprecian. Jean Goldkette, más empresario que músico, reúne a Bix, Tram, Venuti, Lang, los Dorsey, Nichols y el arreglista Bill Challis: en 1926 barre a la banda de Fletcher Henderson en un duelo y Rex Stewart la llama «la primera banda blanca de swing». Paul Whiteman, autoproclamado «rey del jazz» (Robert Goffin dedica en 1931 su libro a «Louis Armstrong, el verdadero rey del jazz»), encarga la Rhapsody in Blue a Gershwin, vende millones con «Whispering» y arreglos pseudoclásicos, pero también da cabida a Bix, a los arreglos de Challis («Changes») y a Bing Crosby, que inventa el canto íntimo de la era del micrófono. Para Gioia, la pureza en la música es un mito.

Este conjunto presenta al oyente un enigma más misterioso si cabe que el de Goldkette. mentions.author: Ted Gioia

Este enfoque resulta especialmente poco indicado cuando se trata de un artista que, como Whiteman, operó principalmente en los intersticios existentes entre diferentes tipos de música. Esto quizá no sería un problema tan importante si los géneros…

Pero las credenciales jazzísticas de la banda de Whiteman también eran considerables. Tomó los mejores efectivos de la orquesta de Goldkette (Beiderbecke, Trumbauer, Challis, Venuti, Lang, Brown) y les sumó numerosos jóvenes talentos, desde Bing Crosby hasta Ferde Grofé. Lo mismo ocurre con las obras de Victor Herbert promocionadas por Whiteman, así como con los arreglos pseudoclásicos de piezas como el «Vals de la Viuda Alegre» de Lehár y el Liebestraum de Liszt. podcast.title: Big Band Leader
podcast.body: Paul Whiteman was a prominent band leader during the Big Band era of jazz, leading large orchestras of ten or more musicians. These leaders were the stars, with all other musicians and singers functioning as employees under their rigid direction. "These were orchestras of ten or more people led by a big name, Paul Whiteman, Tommy Dorsey, Benny Goodman, and so on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: King of Jazz Title
podcast.body: Whiteman earned the title "King of Jazz" by leading a large, 35-musician, all-white band, which contrasted with typical jazz bands of 8-10 improvising musicians. His band played from written charts, essentially cleaning up jazz and making it more palatable for polite society. "Whiteman was a violin player and conductor, and he became known as the King of Jazz for being the band leader of an all-white band of musicians."

xref.title: Big Band Leader
xref.body: Tommy Dorsey was a significant band leader during the Big Band era, leading large orchestras in which he was the central figure. His musicians and singers were employees, following his precise instructions. "These were orchestras of ten or more people led by a big name, Paul Whiteman, Tommy Dorsey, Benny Goodman, and so on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Big Band Leader
xref.body: Benny Goodman was recognized as a major band leader in the Big Band jazz scene. He directed large ensembles, and under the Big Band structure, all performers were subservient to the leader's artistic and musical authority. "These were orchestras of ten or more people led by a big name, Paul Whiteman, Tommy Dorsey, Benny Goodman, and so on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Kurt Cobain's Vaguely Canadian Ancestry
xref.body: Kurt was born on February 20, 1967, at Aberdeen Community Hospital in Aberdeen, Washington. His paternal ancestry traces to a family from Skytown, County Tyrone, Ireland (spelled "Cobane"), who emigrated around 1875 to Cornwall, Ontario, where patriarch Samuel Cobain worked as a shoemaker. Census records confirm a Samuel Cobain, wife, and seven children in Cornwall. They subsequently moved to Gray's Harbor County, Washington, where Aberdeen is located. Kurt's great-uncle Delbert, on his mother's side, was a respected Irish tenor who appears in the 1930 film *King of Jazz* featuring Paul Whiteman and the young Bing Crosby. "Hardly qualifies Kurt as Cancon, but it is still kind of cool."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
